With "loro", the stress does NOT fall on the ending: PAR-la-no, LA-vo-ra-no, ABI-ta-no. Typical mistake: "par-LA-no".
In "capisco" you hear "sk", but in "capisci" you hear "sh": ca-PI-shi. Likewise: finisco / finisci.
QU = a quick "kw", like one sound: quadro = "kwadro", quattro = "kwattro", qui = "kwi".
Italian has an open "e" (bene, tè) and a closed one (francese, perché). Don't worry: everyone will understand you with a Romanian "e".
Italian verbs are divided by their infinitive ending: -ARE (parlare), -ERE (prendere), -IRE (dormire). For the present, you drop the ending and add another one, depending on the person.
Most verbs are -ARE verbs and they're all regular (with a few exceptions: andare, fare, dare, stare). If you learn "parlare", you know hundreds of verbs.
Verbs in -care and -gare keep the hard sound with an H: cercare → cerchi, cerchiamo; pagare → paghi, paghiamo.
The differences are small: -ERE has -ete for "voi", -IRE has -ite. Otherwise the endings are the same. Other verbs: vivere, leggere, scrivere; partire, sentire, aprire.
Many -IRE verbs add -isc- for io, tu, lui/lei and loro. You can't tell in advance which ones: you learn them one by one (capire, finire, preferire, pulire).
The survival sentence: "Non capisco. Può ripetere, per favore?" (I don't understand. Could you repeat that, please?). With friends: "Puoi ripetere?".

The name of the language is usually the same as the masculine adjective: italiano, rumeno, francese, inglese, spagnolo, tedesco. After "parlare" it's usually said without the article: "Parlo italiano".

The typical Romanian mistake: "Abito in Firenze". With cities you use "a": "Abito a Firenze".
"Da" + time = "for / since" (a period that continues): "Vivo a Firenze da una settimana" = "I've been living in Florence for a week".
Where does the stress fall in "lavorano"?
With "loro", the stress stays on the stem.

Professor Bellini is sixty. He's Florentine and has been working in the restoration workshop for thirty years.
He arrives every morning at ten sharp. He doesn't talk much. He reads the newspaper, has a coffee and looks at the paintings.
Today he looks at Matei's work. Matei is cleaning a little angel from the Seicento, very slowly, with a fine brush.
Giulia waits. Matei waits. The professor says nothing for two minutes.
Then he says just one word: "Good." And he leaves.
Giulia laughs: "Matei, you don't understand! The professor says 'good' once a year!"
That evening Matei writes to his sister: "Ilinca, my boss said 'good'. I'm very happy."
